This week's progress is a continuation to our discussion last week where
JD had brought up the idea of using a truncated quadratic distribution
and further explored this idea with Copilot. On my own, I had prompted
Copilot for a similar idea, where it had suggested to use Legendre
Polynomials to perform a Neyman Smoothness Test. When implementing this,
I used the first six basis functions along with normalization of the
basis coefficients so that they would follow a known Standard Normal
distribution. Since the basis functions are orthonormal, this indicates
that we can construct individual SlugPlots for these coefficients, which
have value zero under the null hypothesis that the p-values are uniform.
However, typical inference on these coefficients is done by considering
the squared sum of the normalized coefficients, where the test statistic
follows a chi-squared distribution with the degrees of freedom being the
number of coefficients that were estimated. This joint inference tests
whether the additional coefficients are equal to 0. Such tests are
called Neyman Smoothness Tests. I have these notes written down in my
book, but this description should suffice.

This .Rmd performs these smoothness tests. In particular, I revisit the
t-test case that we previously had trouble with. From my analysis, it
seems like this test is VERY powerful and gives strong signals against
uniformity even when the p-values are generated from a Beta(0.95, 1).
Although I hadn't mentioned it previously (since JD is already aware),
modelling our p-values with these polynomials increases the range of
shapes that we can perform our analysis on, primarily bimodal p-values.
The code below demonstrates this ability.

Also, I asked Copilot to compare the Legendre and Truncated Quadratic.
It said they were very similar, but did prefer the Neyman Test.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Imports
source("legendre_Fun.R")
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# Base Configurations
n.neyman <- 5000; n.legendre <- 1000; n.t.list <- c(10,100)
```

\newpage

For example, the code below shows how it is strongly flagging a
Beta(0.95, 1) against uniformity. I think this is a good thing, however,
one might worry that it is too strong (if that makes any sense)? By
looking at the individual pianos for the coefficients, we can identify
which shape is contributing to the non-uniformity.

```{r}
pvals <- matrix(rbeta(n = n.neyman*n.legendre, shape1 = 0.95, shape2 = 1)
                , nrow = n.legendre)
lc <- legendre.coef(pvals)
lp <- legendre.pval(n.legendre, lc, "two")
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=7}
par(mfrow = c(3,1))

hist(lp[,"joint"], breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41), 
     main = "Neyman Smoothness Test", xlab = "p")

hist(lp[,"theta1"], breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41), 
     main = "P-Values for Coefficient of Theta1", xlab = "p")

hist(lp[,"theta6"], breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41), 
     main = "P-Values for Coefficient of Theta6", xlab = "p")
```

\newpage

For verification, here is what happens when the p-values are uniform.

```{r}
pvals <- matrix(rbeta(n = n.neyman*n.legendre, shape1 = 1, shape2 = 1)
                , nrow = n.legendre)
lc <- legendre.coef(pvals)
lp <- legendre.pval(n.legendre, lc, "two")
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=7}
par(mfrow = c(3,1))

hist(lp[,"joint"], breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41), 
     main = "Neyman Smoothness Test", xlab = "p")

hist(lp[,"theta1"], breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41), 
     main = "P-Values for Coefficient of Theta1", xlab = "p")

hist(lp[,"theta2"], breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41), 
     main = "P-Values for Coefficient of Theta2", xlab = "p")
```

\newpage

```{r fig.height=6, fig.width=7}
# ----- Config 1: df = 2
set.seed(1)
df2 <- legendre.wrap(n.neyman, n.legendre, n.t.list, "t", 
              dist.args = list(df = 2), chunk.neyman = 1000, 
              t.p.out = "left", ney.p.out = "left")
```

\newpage

Also, we might have a preference on which p-values we output from the
t-test (and neyman test). If we recall the bimodal piano for the t-test,
those p-values were from the left-tailed (signed) approach. However, if
we made it so the t-test outputs a two-tailed p-value, then the bimodal
structure doesn't appear. This should be noted, however this doesn't
give us reason to go back to the Beta approach since we want a method
that can handle all p-value structures. Example below:

```{r fig.height=6, fig.width=4}
par(mfrow = c(2,1))
set.seed(1)
pv <- tTest.pvalRaw(5000, 10, "t", dist.args = list(df = 2), t.p.out = "left")
hist(pv, breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41))
set.seed(1)
pv <- tTest.pvalRaw(5000, 10, "t", dist.args = list(df = 2), t.p.out = "two")
hist(pv, breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41))
```

\newpage

Also also, one might think that the raw t-test p-values in the upper
rows of the panels may not look uniform when df = 15 or 30. This is
because there are only 1000 points being plotted. If we increase that to
better observe the distribution, we obtain the following:

```{r fig.height=3, fig.width=5}
set.seed(1)
pv <- tTest.pvalRaw(10000, 10, "t", dist.args = list(df = 30), t.p.out = "left")
hist(pv, breaks = seq(0,1,length.out = 41))
```
